summary: This unit teaches you to provide bell services: receiving arriving guests and their luggage, lifting and loading safely, escorting guests to rooms, storing luggage with claim tags, helping guests depart, moving luggage in a room change, delivering messages and parcels, running errands, giving honest information and keeping guests and their belongings secure.

blocks.p: This unit covers the work of the bell team at a hotel, resort or large villa property: meeting guests when they arrive, handling their luggage, taking them to their rooms, storing bags, helping them leave, delivering messages and parcels, running errands, giving directions and keeping an eye on security. It is for HOSPITALITY VILLA/PROPERTIES SERVICES LEVEL 2 trainees.

Bell staff are often the **first and last** people a guest meets, and they handle the guest's most personal belongings. A friendly greeting, careful hands and honest, accurate records build trust. A dropped bag, a lost tag or a careless word about a room number can ruin a stay.

What this means on the job

Be well groomed, with a clean uniform and name badge
Receive arriving guests and their luggage
Greet, help out of the car, unload, count and tag the bags
Check for damage and take the guests to the desk and to their room
Handle luggage safely
Lift, carry and load correctly; use trolleys; get help with heavy bags
Store luggage
Use claim tags, a locked room and the storage log

Collect luggage, check the room, check the bill, load the car and count again
Move luggage when a guest changes rooms

Deliver messages, parcels and run errands

flow: Meet at the entrance
Unload, count and tag the bags
Escort to the desk and the room
Store luggage if the room is not ready
Deliver messages and run errands during the stay
Collect luggage and load the car at departure

blocks.note: How you are assessed: two theory papers (multiple-choice questions, short answers and essays) and two practical tasks. In the first you receive arriving guests, handle and store luggage with claim tags and return it. In the second you handle a departure and deliver a message, a parcel and letters, including a room with a Do Not Disturb sign. The assessor watches your safe lifting, counting, records and manner.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.note: In practical work, use only made-up guest names and details, and keep the car's engine off during role play.
blocks.label: Safety

sections.title: The bell team and the bell desk

head: Job
Main duties
rows: Bell captain
Leads the team on the shift, gives out jobs, checks the log, deals with problems and reports to the front office manager
Bell attendant (bellperson)
Handles luggage, escorts guests to rooms, stores bags, delivers messages and parcels, runs errands
Doorman
Stands at the main entrance, greets guests, opens car doors and calls taxis
Concierge
Gives guests information and books tours, transport and restaurants
Front desk agent
Checks guests in and out and gives the key; works closely with the bell desk
Security officer
Keeps guests, staff and property safe

blocks.p: At small villas one person may do several of these jobs. Learn what your property expects of you, and keep to the chain of command: take your jobs from the bell captain and report problems to your supervisor.

ol: Be on time. Your **uniform** must be clean and pressed, shoes polished, hair and nails tidy, and your **name badge** worn.
Read the **bell log** and the handover from the last shift: luggage in storage, errands not finished, guests expecting help.
Check the **arrivals and departures lists** to see how busy the day will be and which guests need special help (VIPs, elderly guests, groups).
Check the equipment: luggage trolleys (wheels, rails, brakes), claim tags, luggage tags, errand cards, the bell log, pens, umbrellas, radio or phone and a torch.
Check the **luggage storage room** is locked and that the stored bags match the log.
Make sure the entrance area and the bell desk are clean and tidy.

blocks.note: Bell staff are often the first people a guest meets. Your grooming and manner create the first impression of the property.
blocks.label: Remember

head: Item
Used for
rows: Luggage trolley (bell cart)
Moving several bags at once; has a top rail for garment bags
Luggage tags
Fastened to each bag with the guest's name and room number
Two-part claim tags
One part on the bag, one part (the stub) given to the guest, with the same number
Bell log (bell sheet)
Records each arrival, departure, storage, errand and message
Errand card
Records an errand: what, for whom, who did it, time, money given and receipt
Radio or phone
Keeping in touch with the desk while you move around the property
Umbrella
Keeping guests and their bags dry in the rain

blocks.note: Team Jamaica training for people who work with visitors is run by the Tourism Product Development Company (TPDCo). Its message is warm, honest and professional service for every visitor.
blocks.label: Jamaica

sections.title: Receiving arriving guests and their luggage

flow: Go to the car and greet the guests
Help them out of the vehicle
Unload the luggage carefully
Count the bags with the guest and check for damage
Check nothing is left in the car
Load the trolley correctly and tag the bags
Escort the guests to the desk

ul: Go to the car **promptly**, with a smile: 'Good afternoon, welcome to Jamaica. Let me help you with your bags.'
Open the door and help guests out, especially elderly guests, children and anyone with difficulty walking.
In rain, meet them with an **umbrella** and cover the luggage.
Check the car, the back seat and the boot so that no bag is left behind.
Ask which bags are **fragile** or valuable, and handle those with special care.

blocks.p: **Count the bags with the guest.** Say the number aloud: 'That is four bags, a suitcase, two small bags and a garment bag. Is that correct?' Look at each bag as you lift it. If you see damage, such as a broken handle, a torn corner or a dent, **point it out to the guest at once** and note it in the log. This protects you from being blamed later.

ul: Put **heavy bags at the bottom and the back**, and lighter bags on top.
Hang **garment bags on the top rail** so that they do not crush.
Do not stack so high that you cannot see ahead. Do not overload.
Place fragile items on top or carry them by hand, as the guest asks.
Tag each bag with the guest's name and the room number, once the room is known.

blocks.p: Take guests to the front desk and stay with the luggage. Never leave bags unattended. When the guest has the key, escort them to the room, carrying the bags.

ol: Walk slightly ahead. Show the way, the lift and anything useful on the route.
At the door, **knock and announce** 'Bell service', even if you know the room is empty.
Open the door, switch on the lights and put the bags on the luggage rack, or where the guest wants them.
**Give a short tour**: air conditioner, lights, safe, mini bar, telephone, curtains and balcony door, and how to use the key card.
Tell them about the pool, the restaurants and the times. Ask, 'Is there anything else I can do for you?'
Leave quietly and politely. **Never ask for a tip.**
Return the trolley and note the job in the bell log.

blocks.note: Never say the room number aloud in the lobby or in the car park. Check it on the key folder.
blocks.label: Safety

blocks.h: If the room is not ready

blocks.p: Guests who arrive early may have to wait. **Tag the luggage, give the guest the stub and lock the bags in the luggage room.** Tell the guest about the lobby, the pool and the restaurants. When the room is ready, the desk will tell you, and you take the bags up, or deliver them if the guests have gone out.

blocks.note: Do not take a guest's bag into a room that is not yet cleaned and inspected.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: Lifting and carrying luggage is the most common cause of injury to bell staff. A bad back can end your career, and a dropped bag can injure a guest. Learn safe methods now.

ol: **Look at the bag** and test its weight by tilting it. If it is too heavy or awkward, get help or use a trolley.
Stand close, with your feet apart, one slightly forward.
**Bend your knees** and keep your **back straight**. Do not bend from the waist.
Get a firm grip on the handles or the bottom corners.
Lift with your legs, keeping the load **close to your body**.
Do not twist. Turn by moving your feet.
Put the bag down the same way, with your knees bent.

head: Do
Do not
rows: Plan the lift and the path before you move
Rush or take the bag without looking
Use a trolley for more than two bags
Carry bags in a way that blocks your view
Get a colleague to help with a heavy trunk or odd shape
Try to lift something that is too heavy for you alone
Keep paths and doors clear
Leave bags in walkways where someone can trip
Wear sensible, non-slip shoes
Wear shoes that are loose or slippery

blocks.p: Heavy suitcases may be around 20 to 30 kg: airlines usually allow about 23 kg for each checked bag, but this varies. Weights are in **kilograms** in Jamaica. If a bag feels too heavy, treat it as too heavy. Ask for help.

ul: Push it at a **steady pace**, so that you can see ahead and stop. Do not run.
Go slowly round corners and on ramps. Keep it under control on slopes.
Use the lift as the property's rules say; keep your hands inside.
Do not leave a loaded trolley in a walkway or on a slope.
Garment bags hang on the top rail so they do not crease.

head: Item
How to handle it
rows: Fragile items (marked or said to be fragile)
Carry by hand or put on top; never stack anything on them
Garment and suit bags
Hang them on the trolley rail; keep them off the floor
Golf clubs, surfboards and sports kit
Handle with care; ask where the guest wants them; use the proper storage
Pushchairs and car seats
Open and close carefully; keep small parts together
Very heavy trunks and cases
Two people, or a trolley with straps

ul: Put **heavy cases first at the bottom**, and small bags and soft bags on top.
Do not force the boot closed. Leave fragile and valuable items for the guest to carry or to sit on the back seat.
Close the boot gently with your fingers clear of the edge.
Count the bags again with the guest at the car.

blocks.note: Move away from moving vehicles. Never walk behind a reversing car. In the driveway, stay on the side and in clear view of drivers.
blocks.label: Safety

blocks.p: Guests may want to leave luggage before check-in, after check-out, or while they travel. Storing luggage safely is an important trust. You are responsible for the bags in your care.

flow: Count the bags with the guest
Advise that valuables go in the safe deposit box
Attach a two-part claim tag: one part on the bag, the stub to the guest
Record the bags in the storage log
Place bags in the locked luggage room
Keep the room locked at all times

ul: Before you accept bags, ask whether they contain **cash, jewellery, passports, electronics or medicine**. Advise the guest to put valuables in the safe deposit box.
Write on the tag: the guest's name, the number of bags, the date and the tag number. The stub has the same number.
In the log, write: the date and time, the guest's name, the number of bags, a description and the tag number, and your name.
Group bags together by guest and in a set order, so you can find them quickly. Keep fragile items on top and heavy ones at the bottom.
Keep the luggage room locked. Keep the key with the bell captain or the authorised person, and sign it out.

head: Situation
What to do
rows: The person has the matching stub
Match the numbers, check the bags, hand them over, and write the time, stub number and the name of the person who collected them in the log
The person has lost the stub
Do not hand the bags over until you have checked the person's identity and followed the procedure; the guest or desk may need to confirm; ask the person to sign
Someone else comes for the bags
Only release them if the guest has agreed and the procedure is followed; never on a verbal claim alone
Bags are not collected
Follow the policy: after a set time they are moved to lost property and the guest is contacted

blocks.note: If you hand a bag to the wrong person, the property may have to pay and you may lose your job. Never rush at a busy time. Check the stub.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: Valuables left in bags are risky. The luggage room is not a safe. Advise guests to carry their passports, medicines, money, cameras and phones with them, or use the safe deposit box.

blocks.h: A guest who wants a bag watched

blocks.p: Never agree to 'watch my bags' for a few minutes in a lobby or at an entrance. Either keep them in sight (if you are on duty at the desk), or tag and store them. A bag left alone might be taken, or a person might say it is theirs.

flow: Take the request (room, number of bags, time) and log it
Go to the room on time; knock and announce
Count the bags with the guest
Remind the guest to check drawers, wardrobe, safe and bathroom
Take the luggage to the lobby
Check with the desk that the bill is settled
Load the car; count the bags again with the guest
Say goodbye, and record the departure

ul: When a guest phones the bell desk, ask for the **room number, the number of bags and the time** they want you. Write it in the log.
Go to the room on time. **Knock and announce**: 'Bell service.' Wait for the guest to open the door.
Count the bags and say the number. Ask the guest to look in the **drawers, wardrobe, safe and bathroom**.
Take the bags down by lift or by trolley. Do not leave them unattended in the lobby.
**Check with the front desk that the bill has been settled** before you load the luggage. If it has not, ask the guest to visit the desk.
Load the car safely. At the car, **count the bags again** with the guest, so that they confirm nothing is left behind.
Wish them a safe trip. Write the departure in the log with the time.

blocks.p: If you find an item in a room after the guest has left, such as a phone charger, **do not keep it**. Take it to the lost property room, log it with the date, room and your name, and tell the front desk so they can try to contact the guest.

ul: Ask the time of the flight and the transport booked. Many guests leave about 3 hours before an international flight.
Ask the guest to be ready at the time the driver is booked.
If the guest is early, tag and store the bags, or keep them in sight.

blocks.p: A guest may move from one room to another because of a fault, noise or an upgrade. The front desk gives you a **room change slip** and the new key.

ol: Get the room change slip and the new key from the front desk.
Move the guest's things with the **guest present**. If the guest is out, the move is done with a supervisor or security to witness it.
Check the old room: wardrobe, drawers, bathroom and under the beds, so nothing is left.
Do not open the guest's safe. Ask the guest to empty it.
Place the items in the new room as neatly as they were, and show the guest the room.
Return the old key to the desk, tell housekeeping and write the move in the log.

blocks.note: Never go into a guest's room without a reason, and never touch items that you are not told to move. If the guest is out, ask security or a supervisor to be with you.
blocks.label: Safety

ol: Check the item, the guest's name and the room number on the desk's slip.
Go to the room. **Knock, say who you are** ('Bell service') and wait.
Hand the item to the guest. Do not push it under the door or leave it outside.
If there is no answer, return it to the desk and note it in the log. The desk can leave a note or switch on the message light.
Write the job in the bell log, with the time.

blocks.p: If the door has a **Do Not Disturb (DND) sign**, do not knock. Tell the desk so they can pass the message another way, such as the telephone, an envelope under the door or a note at the desk.

Write messages clearly with the **date, time, the caller's name and number, the guest's name and the message**. Read it back to the caller. Sign it with your name. A message that cannot be read or is incomplete is useless.

ul: Fill in an **errand card**: the job, the guest's name and room, the time, the money given and the receipt.
Count any money in front of the guest. Bring back the **change and the receipt**.
If a guest asks you to post letters, log it, post them promptly and tell the guest. Stamps cost money: note the amount.
Never use a guest's money for yourself. Never agree to anything illegal or unsafe, such as buying illegal drugs.
Report any problem to the bell captain.

blocks.note: Errand cards and the bell log are your proof: they show what you did, when, and with what money. They protect the guest, the property and you.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: Guests ask for directions, restaurants, shops, beaches and attractions. Know the area around your property and the main sights, and keep a map and local information at the bell desk. If you are not sure, say 'Let me check' and ask the concierge or the tour desk. **Never guess.**

head: Request
Good answer
rows: How to get to a waterfall or an attraction
Clear directions, the usual time by car, opening times and the cost; offer licensed transport
A restaurant recommendation
A few good places and their opening hours; ask what food the guest likes and the budget
Changing money
The front desk or a licensed cambio (currency exchange). Do not change money yourself or send guests to street dealers
Weather for a trip
Check a reliable forecast, or ask the tour desk; do not guess, especially for boat trips
Safe walking and going out at night
Give friendly safety tips: use licensed taxis, keep valuables hidden and stay in well-lit areas

ul: Call only **taxis that the property approves**. Licensed drivers have been checked and are insured. In Jamaica licensed public passenger vehicles carry red number plates, and tourist taxis are often linked to an association such as JUTA.
Give the driver the guest's destination. Agree the fare before the journey if the property's policy says so.
Write down the taxi's number plate or the driver's name for the guest's safety, as the property's policy states.
Never take money or gifts from drivers for sending guests to them.

blocks.note: Guests will often ask what is safe and what is not. Be honest and calm. Do not frighten the guest, and do not hide real risks, such as strong currents on a beach or a storm warning.
blocks.label: Jamaica

ul: **Room numbers are private.** If a visitor asks which room a guest is in, do not give it. Offer to call the guest from the desk.
Never let a stranger into a room, even if they say they lost the key. Send them to the front desk to show who they are.
Never leave luggage unattended. Count bags at every handover.
Keep the luggage room locked. Return bags only against the stub, or after checking ID.
Report suspicious people or behaviour to security and the supervisor at once.

blocks.p: A bag left alone in the lobby or at the entrance for a long time could be a danger. **Do not touch or move it.** Ask nearby people whether it belongs to them. If nobody claims it, tell security at once and keep people away, following the property's emergency procedure.

ul: When a guest or staff member hands in an item, such as a wallet or a phone, **record it** with the date, time, place found and the finder's name.
Hand it to lost property or security. Never keep it yourself or look through it alone.
When the owner collects it, ask for a description and a signature, and write the date and time.

blocks.p: A guest phones to say that one of her bags did not reach her room.

flow: Apologise and stay calm
Get a description of the bag and the room
Check the bell log for the count and who delivered it
Search the likely places and ask colleagues
Keep the guest informed
Report to the supervisor and security if it is not found, and record it

ul: Always **apologise**, even if it was not your fault. Listen, and do not blame others.
Do not promise the bag will be found. Say what you are doing.
If the bag is found, deliver it with an apology and write it in the log.

blocks.note: Jamaica's emergency numbers: police 119; ambulance and fire service 110. Know the property's emergency plan, the exits and the assembly point.
blocks.label: Jamaica

blocks.p: A guest may give a tip as a thank-you. Accept politely and say 'Thank you very much'. Never ask for a tip, never show disappointment, and follow the property's rules on sharing tips and on money.

ul: describe the jobs of the bell captain, bell attendant, doorman and concierge
prepare for the shift and check the trolleys, tags, log and radio
greet arriving guests, help them out, unload and count the bags with them
point out damage and handle fragile bags and garment bags correctly
load a trolley and a car boot correctly
lift and carry safely, and know when to get help
escort a guest to the room, knock and announce, and show the room features
store luggage with a two-part claim tag, the log and the locked luggage room
return stored bags only against the stub or after checking ID
help a guest to depart: count, check the room, check the bill, load and count again
move a guest's belongings during a room change using the slip
deliver messages and parcels, respecting Do Not Disturb
complete an errand card and the bell log
give honest directions and suggest only licensed, approved transport
keep room numbers private and deal with an unattended bag, a lost item or a missing bag

terms: Bell captain
The leader of the bell team on a shift
Bell attendant
A staff member who handles guests' luggage and runs errands
Doorman
The staff member who greets guests at the main entrance
Concierge
The staff member who gives information and books tours, transport and restaurants
Porte cochère
The covered entrance where cars stop to drop guests off
Claim tag and stub
A two-part tag: one part on the bag and the matching stub kept by the guest
Bell log
The record of arrivals, departures, storage and errands
Errand card
The slip that records an errand, with times and money
Do Not Disturb (DND)
A sign that tells staff not to knock or enter
Room change slip
The form that allows the bell team to move a guest's luggage to another room
Lost property
Items found and held until the owner collects them
Cambio
A licensed place that changes foreign currency

c1.title: A family arrives in the rain at Montego Bay
c1.text: The Brown family arrive at a hotel in Montego Bay at 5 p.m. in a taxi, in heavy rain. They have a large suitcase, two medium bags, a garment bag with two suits, and a box marked 'fragile' that holds a wedding gift. The father, Mr Dennis Brown, says the box is the most important thing they have brought. One handle on the large suitcase is hanging loose. Their room will be ready in about an hour.

c2.title: Luggage storage before a late flight
c2.text: Mrs Sandra Francis checks out of a villa property at 11 a.m. but her flight leaves at 8 p.m. She asks the bell desk to keep her two suitcases and a small bag for the day. She says the small bag has her laptop and jewellery. Bell attendant Omar is working alone, and the luggage room has a lock and a log. At 4 p.m. a man comes to the desk saying he is her husband and has lost the stub.

c3.title: A departure with a room check
c3.text: Mr and Mrs Reid call the bell desk at 9:30 a.m. to help with their bags at check-out. They have four bags. Omar goes to the room, knocks, and counts the bags. Mrs Reid says they are ready, but Omar sees a pair of sunglasses on the bedside table. The guests' taxi has arrived, and Mr Reid says he already settled the bill at the desk yesterday.

c4.title: Messages, a parcel and a trip request
c4.text: The bell desk at a resort in Negril is given a written message for a guest in room 214, a parcel for a guest in room 118 and a request from Mrs Palmer to post three letters. Room 214 has a Do Not Disturb sign. A guest, Mr Hylton, also asks the attendant to recommend a restaurant and to call a taxi for a trip to a beach 20 minutes away. The attendant knows two licensed taxis on the property's approved list. A man in a car at the gate offers money to send guests to him.

c5.title: A quiet afternoon with some concerns
c5.text: At 3 p.m. in the lobby, a black backpack sits alone beside a pillar. Nobody is near it, and it has been there for 40 minutes. Later a visitor who is not a guest says he is a guest's cousin and asks Omar to take a gift up to her room. A guest, Ms Clarke, phones the bell desk to say one of her two suitcases did not reach her room after arrival.

questions.q: The Browns' taxi stops at the entrance in the rain. What should the attendant do first?
o: Go to the taxi with an umbrella, greet the family and help them out
Wait under the porch and let the family bring their bags in themselves
Call the front desk to ask which room the Browns have booked
Unload the bags first, then greet the family once they are inside
questions.why: Go to the vehicle promptly and welcome the guests, covering them and their luggage from the rain. The people come first, then the luggage.

questions.q: What should the attendant do about the loose handle on the large suitcase?
o: Say nothing, since the damage was there before the family arrived
Point it out to Mr Brown at once and note it in the log
Fix it with tape, then tell the guest at the end of the day
Tell the family only if they ask about the suitcase later
questions.why: Damage seen at arrival must be pointed out to the guest and noted, so the property is not blamed for it later.

questions.q: How should the garment bag and the fragile box be handled on the trolley?
o: The garment bag lies flat on the trolley floor, under the heavy cases
The box goes on the bottom of the trolley, where it cannot fall over
The garment bag hangs on the top rail; the box is carried by hand
Both are packed tightly between the suitcases, so they cannot move
questions.why: Garment bags hang on the top rail, and fragile items go on top, or are carried, with nothing placed on them.

questions.q: The room will not be ready for an hour. What should happen to the luggage?
o: It is left by the desk, where the attendant can see it all the time
It is taken to the room and left outside the door for the guests
It is kept in the taxi until the room is ready, to save handling it
It is tagged, the guest gets a stub, and the bags are locked away
questions.why: Tag and store luggage in a locked room, and give the guest the stub. Bags in a lobby or a corridor can be taken or mixed up.

questions.q: What should Omar advise Mrs Francis about her small bag with the laptop and jewellery?
o: Put them in the safe deposit box or take them with her
Leave them in the bag, since the luggage room is always locked
Put the bag at the top of the pile, where it can easily be seen
Write 'valuables' on the tag, so that staff will take extra care
questions.why: The luggage room is not a safe. Valuables, cash and electronics should go in the safe deposit box or stay with the guest.

questions.q: What does Omar write on the claim tag and in the storage log?
o: Only the room number the guest had, since that is enough to identify her
The guest's name, number of bags, date and tag number, and his own name in the log
The time she is leaving for the airport and the number of her flight home
The weight of each bag in kilograms and the guest's passport number
questions.why: The tag and log record the name, number of bags, date and tag number, so the right bags can be found and matched to the stub.

questions.q: At 4 p.m. a man says he is Mrs Francis's husband and has lost the stub. What should Omar do?
o: Release the bags, because the man knows her name and her flight times
Ask him to describe the bags, then release them if his answer is correct
Not release the bags until the procedure is followed and the desk confirms
Ask him to sign a note on the spot, and then let him take the bags
questions.why: Bags are released only against the stub or after the procedure, with identity and confirmation checked. A description is not proof.

questions.q: When Mrs Francis returns for her bags with the correct stub, what should Omar record?
o: Only the time, since the stub number is already in the log
The name of the taxi driver who is waiting for her
The tip that Mrs Francis gives him for looking after the bags
The time, the stub number and who collected the bags
questions.why: The log must show when the bags left, which stub matched and who took them. It proves the bags were returned correctly.

questions.q: Omar sees sunglasses on the bedside table. What should he do?
o: Point them out to the guests and ask if they have everything
Put them in his pocket and give them in at the end of the shift
Leave them there, since the guests have already said they are ready
Take them to lost property without telling the guests
questions.why: Reminding the guest to check the room prevents lost items. If they are not the guests', they go to lost property and are logged.

questions.q: Before loading the bags into the taxi, what should Omar check?
o: With the guests, that they have booked the taxi themselves
With the front desk, that the bill has been settled
With the driver, that the boot is large enough for all bags
With security, that the bags have been scanned
questions.why: Luggage is not released until the desk confirms the bill is settled. The guest's word alone is not enough for the record.

questions.q: How should the bags be loaded into the taxi boot?
o: Small bags on the bottom so they are protected by the cases
Whichever order is quickest, as long as the lid closes
Heavy cases at the bottom and small bags on top
Heavy cases at the top, so they are easy to lift out
questions.why: Heavy cases go in first and low down; small and soft bags go on top. This prevents crushing and keeps the load steady.

questions.q: Why does Omar count the bags again at the taxi?
o: So that he can tell the driver how much to charge for the bags
So that he can write the total weight of the bags in the log
So that the guests can see that he has not taken any of the bags
So the guests can confirm that nothing is left behind
questions.why: Counting again at the car, with the guests, confirms that all the bags are loaded and nothing was left in the room, lobby or trolley.

questions.q: Room 214 has a Do Not Disturb sign. What should the attendant do with the written message?
o: Not knock, and tell the desk so it can pass the message another way
Knock softly, because a message may be important to the guest
Push the message under the door and walk away quietly afterwards
Leave it on the door handle, where anyone passing can read it
questions.why: A Do Not Disturb sign means do not knock or enter. The desk can use the phone, a note at the desk or the message light.

questions.q: How should the attendant deliver the parcel to room 118?
o: Leave it outside the door, so that the guest is not disturbed
Knock, say 'Bell service', hand it to the guest and log it
Give it to a housekeeper who is nearby, to deliver on her round
Ask the guest to collect it from the bell desk late the same night
questions.why: Hand items directly to the right guest, then write the job in the log. Parcels left outside a door can be taken.

questions.q: Mrs Palmer asks him to post three letters. What is the correct action?
o: Take them with him and post them when he next goes into town
Tell her that bell staff are not allowed to post letters at all
Fill in an errand card, post them promptly and tell her
Give them to another guest who is going to the post office soon
questions.why: An errand card records the task and cost, and the guest is told when it is done. Delays and unrecorded jobs cause complaints.

questions.q: A man at the gate offers money to send guests to his taxi. What should the attendant do?
o: Accept the money but still send guests to the approved taxis
Accept, since his taxi may well be as good as the other taxis
Ignore him and say nothing to anyone about the offer he made
Refuse politely, use approved taxis and report the offer
questions.why: Staff must give honest advice and never take money from drivers. Report the offer to the supervisor, and use only licensed, approved transport.

questions.q: The backpack has been alone by the pillar for 40 minutes. What is the first thing Omar should do?
o: Not touch it, ask who owns it, and tell security if nobody does
Pick it up and open it to find out who owns it, using the contents
Move it to the bell desk, where it will be safer and can be watched
Wait until the end of the shift to see if anyone comes back for it
questions.why: Do not touch or move an unattended bag. Ask who owns it, and report to security at once if nobody claims it.

questions.q: A visitor says he is a guest's cousin and asks Omar to take a gift up and leave it inside the room. The guest is out. What should Omar do?
o: Take the gift up and leave it on the bed, as the visitor is a relative of hers
Decline to enter, and hand the gift to the desk to tell the guest
Let the visitor go up alone, since it will only take him a minute
Take the visitor's name, and then leave the gift inside the room yourself
questions.why: Staff never enter a guest's room for a visitor, and never let a visitor go up alone. The desk can record the gift and tell the guest when she returns.

questions.q: Ms Clarke says one of her suitcases did not reach her room. What should Omar do first?
o: Tell her it must still be in the taxi and she should phone them
Say the luggage was counted at arrival so nothing can be missing
Apologise, and get a description of the bag and the room
Ask her to come to the lobby to look through all the stored bags
questions.why: Apologise, take the details, then check the bell log for the count and who delivered it. Searching and keeping the guest informed follow.

questions.q: Which of these is the safest way to pick up a heavy suitcase?
o: Bend from the waist and pull the bag up in one quick movement
Twist the body to swing the bag onto the trolley in one move
Lift the bag with one arm, to keep the other hand free
Bend the knees, keep the back straight and lift with the legs
questions.why: Bent knees, a straight back and the load close to the body protect the spine. Twisting or bending from the waist causes injuries.
